title: 218. Algebra, Equations & Inequalities: Logarithmic Equations with Different Bases
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.concept: Converting between bases to solve logarithmic equations
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by changing the base of one logarithm.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2 x=\log_4 9\).
questions.explanation:
Change \(\log_4 9\) to base \(2\):
\[
\log_4 9=\frac{\log_2 9}{\log_2 4}=\frac{2\log_2 3}{2}=\log_2 3
\]
Thus \(\log_2 x=\log_2 3\), so \(x=3\). The domain requires \(x>0\), and \(3>0\), so the solution is valid.
questions.hint: Use the change-of-base formula to write both logarithms with the same base.

questions.concept: Converting between bases to solve logarithmic equations
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by expressing both sides with the same base.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3 x=\log_9 25\).
questions.explanation:
Change \(\log_9 25\) to base \(3\):
\[
\log_9 25=\frac{\log_3 25}{\log_3 9}=\frac{2\log_3 5}{2}=\log_3 5
\]
Thus \(\log_3 x=\log_3 5\), so \(x=5\). Since \(5>0\), it is valid.
questions.hint: Rewrite \(\log_9 25\) as a logarithm base \(3\), then equate the arguments.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting to a common base and applying domain restrictions.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2(x+1)=\log_4(x+7)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+1>0\) and \(x+7>0\), so \(x>-1\). Convert \(\log_4(x+7)\) to base \(2\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_4(x+7) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_2(x+7)\\
\log_2(x+1) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_2(x+7)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(2\log_2(x+1)=\log_2(x+7)\). Therefore \((x+1)^2=x+7\). Expanding gives \(x^2+x-6=0\), so \((x+3)(x-2)=0\). The candidates are \(x=-3\) and \(x=2\). Since the domain requires \(x>-1\), only \(x=2\) is valid.
questions.hint: Convert \(\log_4(x+7)\) to base \(2\), then equate the arguments and check the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting bases and rejecting an extraneous root.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3(x-2)=\log_9(4x-7)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x-2>0\) and \(4x-7>0\), so \(x>2\). Convert \(\log_9(4x-7)\) to base \(3\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_9(4x-7) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_3(4x-7)\\
\log_3(x-2) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_3(4x-7)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(2\log_3(x-2)=\log_3(4x-7)\). Therefore \((x-2)^2=4x-7\). Expanding gives \(x^2-8x+11=0\), so
\[
x=4\pm\sqrt{5}
\]
Since \(4-\sqrt{5}\approx1.76<2\), it is not in the domain. The valid solution is \(x=4+\sqrt{5}\).
questions.hint: Change the base-\(9\) logarithm to base \(3\), solve the resulting quadratic, and reject the root that violates \(x>2\).

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting to base \(5\) and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_5(x+3)=\log_{25}(x^2+5x+9)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+3>0\), so \(x>-3\). Convert \(\log_{25}(x^2+5x+9)\) to base \(5\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_{25}(x^2+5x+9) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_5(x^2+5x+9)\\
\log_5(x+3) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_5(x^2+5x+9)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(2\log_5(x+3)=\log_5(x^2+5x+9)\). Therefore \((x+3)^2=x^2+5x+9\). Expanding gives \(x^2+6x+9=x^2+5x+9\), so \(x=0\). Since \(0>-3\), it is valid. The value \(x=-3\) is not in the domain.
questions.hint: Convert the base-\(25\) logarithm to base \(5\), equate the arguments, and check the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting bases and rejecting a value outside the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_2 x=\log_4(x+6)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x>0\) and \(x+6>0\), so \(x>0\). Convert \(\log_4(x+6)\) to base \(2\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_4(x+6) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_2(x+6)\\
\log_2 x &= \frac{1}{2}\log_2(x+6)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(2\log_2 x=\log_2(x+6)\). Therefore \(x^2=x+6\), so \(x^2-x-6=0\). Factoring gives \((x-3)(x+2)=0\), so \(x=3\) or \(x=-2\). Since the domain requires \(x>0\), only \(x=3\) is valid.
questions.hint: Convert the base-\(4\) logarithm to base \(2\), solve the quadratic, and check that the result is positive.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting to base \(3\) and applying domain restrictions.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3(x-1)=\log_9(2x+1)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x-1>0\) and \(2x+1>0\), so \(x>1\). Convert \(\log_9(2x+1)\) to base \(3\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_9(2x+1) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_3(2x+1)\\
\log_3(x-1) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_3(2x+1)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(2\log_3(x-1)=\log_3(2x+1)\). Therefore \((x-1)^2=2x+1\). Expanding gives \(x^2-2x+1=2x+1\), so \(x^2-4x=0\). Factoring gives \(x(x-4)=0\), so \(x=0\) or \(x=4\). Since the domain requires \(x>1\), only \(x=4\) is valid.
questions.hint: Convert the base-\(9\) logarithm to base \(3\), solve the resulting equation, and reject values outside \(x>1\).

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting to base \(2\) and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_4(x+1)=\log_2(x-1)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+1>0\) and \(x-1>0\), so \(x>1\). Convert \(\log_4(x+1)\) to base \(2\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_4(x+1) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_2(x+1)\\
\frac{1}{2}\log_2(x+1) &= \log_2(x-1)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(\log_2(x+1)=2\log_2(x-1)\). Therefore \(x+1=(x-1)^2\). Expanding gives \(x+1=x^2-2x+1\), so \(x^2-3x=0\). Factoring gives \(x(x-3)=0\), so \(x=0\) or \(x=3\). Since the domain requires \(x>1\), only \(x=3\) is valid.
questions.hint: Convert the base-\(4\) logarithm to base \(2\), then solve the quadratic and check the domain.

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting to base \(5\) and rejecting an extraneous root.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_5(x+4)=\log_{25}(3x+22)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+4>0\) and \(3x+22>0\), so \(x>-4\). Convert \(\log_{25}(3x+22)\) to base \(5\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_{25}(3x+22) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_5(3x+22)\\
\log_5(x+4) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_5(3x+22)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(2\log_5(x+4)=\log_5(3x+22)\). Therefore \((x+4)^2=3x+22\). Expanding gives \(x^2+8x+16=3x+22\), so \(x^2+5x-6=0\). Factoring gives \((x+6)(x-1)=0\), so \(x=-6\) or \(x=1\). Since the domain requires \(x>-4\), only \(x=1\) is valid.
questions.hint: Convert the base-\(25\) logarithm to base \(5\), solve the quadratic, and reject the root that violates \(x>-4\).

questions.concept: Solving logarithmic equations with different bases
questions.learningObjective: Solve a logarithmic equation by converting to base \(3\) and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\log_3(x+5)=\log_9(x^2+9x+24)\).
questions.explanation:
The domain requires \(x+5>0\) and \(x^2+9x+24>0\), so \(x>-5\). Convert \(\log_9(x^2+9x+24)\) to base \(3\) and substitute it into the equation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log_9(x^2+9x+24) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_3(x^2+9x+24)\\
\log_3(x+5) &= \frac{1}{2}\log_3(x^2+9x+24)
\end{aligned}
\]
so \(2\log_3(x+5)=\log_3(x^2+9x+24)\). Therefore \((x+5)^2=x^2+9x+24\). Expanding gives \(x^2+10x+25=x^2+9x+24\), so \(x=-1\). Since \(-1>-5\) and the quadratic argument is \(16>0\), the solution is valid.
questions.hint: Convert the base-\(9\) logarithm to base \(3\), equate the arguments, and check the domain.
